title: When is local Copilot worth it? Three open-weight coders vs. Copilot out of the box
abstract: This session compares three open-weight coding models running locally on an RTX 4090 and Apple M5 with GitHub Copilot’s default agent mode. Attendees will examine benchmark results from real repository tasks and receive a reproducible method for deciding when local inference provides practical value.

Benchmark design, repository tasks, models, and hardware
Results across latency, tool use, and task completion
Workload patterns that favor local models or GitHub Copilot
Reproducing the comparison on your own repositories
keyTakeaways: A repeatable benchmark method for comparing local coding models with GitHub Copilot on real repositories.
A workload decision matrix showing when local inference, Copilot out of the box, or Copilot BYOK is the better fit.

title: Navigating the Grey: Scaling from Single Worker to Multi-VM Undetectable Scrapers
tagline: Building scraping pipelines that hold up against bot defenses at scale.
abstract: Modern web scraping requires navigating strict bot defense systems like Akamai and reCAPTCHA. Extracting data reliably at scale demands an architecture that accurately mimics human behavior for automated problem resolution. This session outlines the technical requirements for building resilient, high throughput scraping pipelines capable of operating undetected over time.
outline: Building: where the data lives, from static HTML and Playwright to the page's own API
Renting or running search and scraping, and levels of OCR
Performance: sync and async, concurrency and parallelism, threads, processes, and the GIL
Scaling out: one job queue, containers, and a Terraform-managed fleet of VMs
Surviving: robots.txt, rate limits, reading failures, and a canary that fails loudly
Undetected: what a site checks, stealth browsers, proxies and IP reputation, extension scraping, burner emails, and CAPTCHA solvers
The greynet challenge: a practice target website
keyTakeaways: Building: look before you scrape, trying the page's own API, then the HTML, then a browser
Performance: overlap the waiting, use processes for parsing, then scale out with one image, one queue, and many VMs
Surviving: start low, back off on 429, and check the content, because a 200 can mean no
Undetected: every layer must agree, with a clean IP, a real browser, and a human pace

title: Navigating the Grey: Building Resilient Python Scrapers That Survive at Scale
tagline: Scraping the store directories of Philippine malls in Python, from the first request to a 53-mall run.
abstract: A talk built on scraping the store directories of Philippine malls. It shows the three places data can live (static HTML, a JavaScript page, the page's own API), takes a 53-mall run from 32.5 s to 2.0 s with asyncio and one process per core, then covers rate limits, proxies, monitoring that fails loudly, and how to decide which barriers to stop at.
outline: What a web scraper is and where it sits in the data value chain
Three doors to the data: static HTML, a JavaScript page, the page's own API
Reading robots.txt before the page
Where the time goes: sync, async, threads, and processes across 53 malls
Rate limits and getting more per request
What a site can see: IP, JavaScript, and proxies
Containerizing the browser stack
PengePassportPH: built-in limits and a canary that fails loudly
Navigating the grey: what a barrier protects and who pays
keyTakeaways: Look before you scrape: the page's own API, then the HTML, then a browser
Overlap the waiting, then use every core: asyncio for the waiting, one process per core for the parsing
They set the bar: start low, back off on errors and Retry-After, and get more per request
Fail loudly: a 200 can mean no, so check every answer and run a check on a schedule
In the grey, ask who pays: what does the barrier protect, and would you sign your name to it?
